```{r, include = FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
```

```{r setup}
suppressPackageStartupMessages(library(modelcompR))
```

This article covers the numerical half of the workflow: how a model becomes
a problem, how `solve()` turns a problem into a solution, what the solution
object holds, how to drive an integrator step by step, how to run ensembles
of simulations, and which of the ported OrdinaryDiffEq.jl methods to pick
for a given problem. The names follow SciMLBase.jl and OrdinaryDiffEq.jl,
so Julia code translates almost line by line.

## Problems from systems

A problem bundles everything a solver needs: the right hand side function,
the initial state `u0`, the parameter vector `p` and the time span. With
ModelingToolkit the function is generated from a compiled `System`, and the
values are given as a list of equations mapping variables to numbers, the
`op` argument (the operating point).

```{r}
t <- t_nounits
D <- D_nounits
variables("x(t)", "y(t)")
parameters("a = 1.5", "b = 1", "g = 3", "d = 1")
lv <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(x) ~ a * x - b * x * y,
                             D(y) ~ -g * y + d * x * y), t, name = "lv"))
prob <- ODEProblem(lv, list(x ~ 1, y ~ 1), c(0, 10))
prob
```

Parameters with a default (`a = 1.5` above) need not appear in `op`.
The numeric fields are plain R vectors. Note that the order of the unknowns
is chosen by structural simplification and need not be the order of
declaration, so code should index by symbol rather than by position.

```{r}
prob$u0
prob$p
prob$tspan
```

### Symbolic indexing of problems

Indexing a problem with a variable returns its initial value, and
`prob$ps[...]` reads a parameter, as `prob[x]` and `prob.ps[a]` in
ModelingToolkit. Any expression of the model can be evaluated at the
initial point too.

```{r}
prob[x]
prob$ps[a]
prob[x * y + a]
```

Assigning through `prob$ps` changes a parameter and returns the updated
problem. modelcompR does not export the SymbolicIndexingInterface getters
and setters (`getu`, `setu`, `getp`, `setp`); the indexing operators above
and `remake()` cover the same ground.

```{r}
prob$ps[a] <- 2
prob$ps[a]
```

### remake

`remake()` returns a modified copy and leaves the original alone. New
values may be partial maps (only the given entries change) or full
numeric vectors; the time span and solver keywords stored in the problem
can be replaced as well.

```{r}
prob2 <- remake(prob, u0 = list(x ~ 2), p = list(g ~ 2.5), tspan = c(0, 5))
c(prob2[x], prob2[y], prob2$ps[g])
prob2$tspan
c(prob[x], prob$ps[g])
```

## Problems from plain R functions

Without a symbolic model, a problem is built from a function `f(u, p, t)`
that returns the derivative, exactly as `ODEProblem(f, u0, tspan, p)` in
SciMLBase. An unnamed fourth argument is the parameter vector.

```{r}
lotka <- function(u, p, t) c(p[1] * u[1] - p[2] * u[1] * u[2],
                             -p[3] * u[2] + p[4] * u[1] * u[2])
fprob <- ODEProblem(lotka, c(1, 1), c(0, 10), c(1.5, 1, 3, 1))
fsol <- solve(fprob, Tsit5())
fsol$u[[length(fsol$t)]]
```

Symbolic indexing needs a system, so for such problems the states are
indexed by position: `fsol[1, ]` is the first state at every saved time.

```{r}
head(fsol[1, ])
```

A mass matrix `M u' = f(u, p, t)` is given with `mass_matrix`; a zero row
makes the corresponding equation algebraic.

```{r}
mprob <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) c(-u[1] + u[2], u[1] + u[2] - 1),
                    c(1, 0), c(0, 1), mass_matrix = diag(c(1, 0)))
msol <- solve(mprob, Rodas5P())
msol$u[[length(msol$t)]]
```

A fully implicit DAE `F(du, u, p, t) = 0` is a `DAEProblem`, which takes the
residual function, initial derivatives `du0`, initial states `u0` and the
time span, and optionally which components are differential.

```{r}
resid <- function(du, u, p, t) c(du[1] - u[2], u[2]^3 + u[2] + u[1]^3 + u[1])
dprob <- DAEProblem(resid, c(-1, -1), c(1, -1), c(0, 2),
                    differential_vars = c(TRUE, FALSE))
dsol <- solve(dprob, DFBDF())
dsol$u[[length(dsol$t)]]
```

`SteadyStateProblem()` asks for the state where the right hand side
vanishes. It takes an ODE problem, a system or a function. Solving it
without an algorithm uses a Newton type root finder, and `DynamicSS()`
integrates to steady state instead.

```{r}
ss <- SteadyStateProblem(function(u, p, t) c(1 - u[1], u[1] - 2 * u[2]), u0 = c(0, 0))
solve(ss)$u
solve(ss, DynamicSS())$u
```

## solve() and its options

`solve(prob, alg, ...)` integrates the problem with algorithm `alg`; when
the algorithm is missing, `DefaultODEAlgorithm()` is used (see below). The
common keywords are those of the DifferentialEquations.jl common solver
options.

* `saveat`: a step (save at every multiple) or a vector of times. Values are
  then interpolated at those times and the solution is no longer dense.
* `save_everystep = FALSE`: save only the start and the end.
* `tstops`: times the integrator must step to exactly, such as known
  discontinuities.
* `dense`: keep the full interpolant (the default when saving every step).
* `reltol`, `abstol`: the relative and absolute error tolerances of the
  adaptive step size controller (defaults `1e-3` and `1e-6`).
* `dt`: the initial step, or the fixed step when `adaptive = FALSE` or the
  method is not adaptive.
* `maxiters`: the maximum number of steps.
* `callback`: event handling (see the events article), plus `dtmin`,
  `dtmax`, `isoutofdomain`, `unstable_check` and the controller settings
  documented in `?solve.ODEProblem`.

```{r}
sol <- solve(prob, Tsit5(), saveat = 1)
sol$t
sol <- solve(prob, Tsit5(), saveat = c(0, 2.5, 10))
sol$t
sol$dense
length(solve(prob, Tsit5(), save_everystep = FALSE)$t)
2.5 %in% solve(prob, Tsit5(), tstops = 2.5)$t
length(solve(prob, RK4(), dt = 0.1, adaptive = FALSE)$t)
```

Tightening the tolerances costs more steps:

```{r}
sapply(c(1e-3, 1e-6, 1e-9), function(tol)
  length(solve(prob, Tsit5(), reltol = tol, abstol = tol)$t))
```

When the step budget runs out, the solve stops early with the return code
`MaxIters` and a warning, which we expect here:

```{r}
short <- suppressWarnings(solve(prob, Tsit5(), maxiters = 5))
short$retcode
```

Unknown keywords are an error of class `CommonKwargError` rather than
being silently ignored, which catches typos such as `relto`. The message
lists every accepted keyword and ends with the offending one;
`kwargshandle = "warn"` turns the error into a warning.

```{r}
msg <- tryCatch(solve(prob, Tsit5(), relto = 1e-8), CommonKwargError = function(e) conditionMessage(e))
tail(strsplit(msg, "\n")[[1]], 1)
```

A callback is passed with `callback`. Here a `PresetTimeCallback` doubles
the prey at `t = 5`; the events article treats callbacks in detail.

```{r}
xi <- match("x(t)", names(prob$u0))
cb <- PresetTimeCallback(5, function(integ) integ$u[xi] <- 2 * integ$u[xi])
csol <- solve(prob, Tsit5(), callback = cb)
csol(c(4.999, 5.001), idxs = x)
```

## The solution object

A solution stores the saved times `sol$t`, the saved states `sol$u` (a
list with one state vector per time, as in Julia), the return code, the
problem, the algorithm and the solver statistics.

```{r}
sol <- solve(prob, Tsit5())
sol
sol$retcode
successful_retcode(sol$retcode)
length(sol$t)
sol$u[[2]]
```

`sol$stats` counts the work done: right hand side evaluations `nf`,
Jacobians `njacs`, linear solves `nsolve`, factorizations `nw`, and
accepted and rejected steps.

```{r}
unlist(sol$stats)
```

### Indexing

`sol[x]` is the time series of a variable, and any symbolic expression of
the model, including observed variables and parameters, can be indexed.
A second index selects saved time points; a list of variables gives a
matrix.

```{r}
head(sol[x])
sol[x, 1:3]
head(sol[a * x - b * x * y])
head(sol[list(x, y)], 3)
```

### Interpolation

Calling the solution as a function evaluates the dense interpolant, the
equivalent of `sol(t)` in Julia. `idxs` selects variables or expressions,
and `deriv` gives derivatives of the interpolant.

```{r}
sol(2.5)
sol(c(1, 2, 3), idxs = x)
sol(2.5, idxs = x, deriv = 1)
```

### Conversion and plotting

`as.data.frame()` and `as.matrix()` give the saved values as a table, with
one column per state (and per observed variable for system problems).
`plot()` draws the dense solution; `idxs` selects variables, and a pair of
variables gives a phase plot.

```{r}
head(as.data.frame(sol), 3)
dim(as.matrix(sol))
plot(sol)
plot(sol, idxs = list(x, y))
```

## The integrator interface

`init()` builds an integrator, the object `solve()` uses internally, and
returns it without integrating; the integrator can then be advanced one
step at a time and modified between steps. These are `init`, `step!`,
`solve!`, `reinit!`, `set_u!` and friends in SciMLBase. In R the
functions that modify the integrator are named without the bang:
`step_integrator()`, `solve_integrator()`, `set_u()`, `set_t()`,
`add_tstop()`, `add_saveat()`, `set_proposed_dt()`, `reinit()` and
`terminate()`.

```{r}
decay <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) -p[1] * u, 1, c(0, 1), 2)
integ <- init(decay, Tsit5())
integ
step_integrator(integ)
c(integ$t, integ$u, integ$dt)
```

`step_integrator(integ, dt, stop_at_tdt = TRUE)` advances by exactly `dt`.
Between steps the state can be changed with `set_u()`, a stop time added
with `add_tstop()`, and `integ$interp(t)` evaluates the interpolant of the
last step.

```{r}
step_integrator(integ, 0.25, stop_at_tdt = TRUE)
integ$t
integ$interp(integ$t - 0.01)
set_u(integ, 2 * integ$u)
add_tstop(integ, 0.8)
rest <- solve_integrator(integ)
rest$t
```

`reinit()` restarts from new initial values, and a loop over
`step_integrator()` gives full control of the integration. `get_du()` is
the current derivative and `terminate()` ends the solve.

```{r}
reinit(integ, u0 = 3)
while (integ$t < 0.5) step_integrator(integ)
c(integ$t, integ$u, get_du(integ))
terminate(integ)
solve_integrator(integ)$retcode
```

## Ensembles

An `EnsembleProblem` solves the same problem many times with variations,
as in DiffEqBase. `prob_func(prob, i, repeat_)` builds trajectory `i`,
typically with `remake()`; `output_func(sol, i)` transforms each solution
and returns a list of the output and a rerun flag; `reduction` combines
batches. The trajectories run serially by default, and
`EnsembleThreads()` or `EnsembleDistributed()` run them on parallel
workers.

```{r}
ens <- EnsembleProblem(decay, prob_func = function(prob, i, repeat_) remake(prob, p = i / 2))
sim <- solve(ens, Tsit5(), trajectories = 10, saveat = 0.1)
length(sim)
sim[[3]](1)
```

The ensemble analysis functions summarize the trajectories at a saved step
(`timestep_*`) or at an arbitrary time through the interpolants
(`timepoint_*`).

```{r}
timestep_mean(sim, 11)
timepoint_meanvar(sim, 0.5)
timepoint_quantile(sim, 0.5, 0.9)
```

`EnsembleSummary()` collects the mean, the variance and two quantiles over
time, and has a plot method that draws the mean with the quantile band
dashed. The axis range follows the mean, so `ylim` is set to show the whole
band.

```{r}
summ <- EnsembleSummary(sim, quantiles = c(0.1, 0.9))
names(summ)
plot(summ, ylim = range(summ$qlow, summ$qhigh))
```

An `output_func` keeps only what is needed; here the final value of each
trajectory, with random initial values drawn from a seeded stream.

```{r}
ens2 <- EnsembleProblem(decay,
  prob_func = function(prob, i, repeat_) remake(prob, u0 = stats::runif(1)),
  output_func = function(sol, i) list(sol$u[[length(sol$t)]], FALSE))
unlist(solve(ens2, Tsit5(), trajectories = 5, seed = 1)$u)
```

## The solver catalog

The algorithms are grouped as in OrdinaryDiffEq.jl. Each constructor
returns an algorithm object whose options are its arguments. For the
examples we use two test problems: a harmonic oscillator, nonstiff, and
a semidiscretized heat equation $u_t = u_{xx}$ on 20 interior grid points,
whose Laplacian has eigenvalues down to about $-4/\Delta x^2$, which makes
it stiff. Its exact solution is a decaying sine with the smallest discrete
eigenvalue as its rate.

```{r}
osc <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) c(u[2], -u[1]), c(1, 0), c(0, 2 * pi))
err <- function(s) max(abs(s$u[[length(s$t)]] - c(1, 0)))

N <- 20
dx <- 1 / (N + 1)
lap <- diag(-2, N)
lap[cbind(1:(N - 1), 2:N)] <- 1
lap[cbind(2:N, 1:(N - 1))] <- 1
lap <- lap / dx^2
xs <- seq_len(N) * dx
lambda1 <- -4 / dx^2 * sin(pi * dx / 2)^2
heat <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) as.vector(lap %*% u), sin(pi * xs), c(0, 0.5))
heat_exact <- exp(lambda1 * 0.5) * sin(pi * xs)
heat_err <- function(s) max(abs(s$u[[length(s$t)]] - heat_exact))

compare <- function(prob, algs, errfun, ...) {
  do.call(rbind, lapply(algs, function(alg) {
    s <- solve(prob, alg, ...)
    data.frame(alg = alg$name, retcode = s$retcode, steps = s$stats$naccept,
               nf = s$stats$nf, error = signif(errfun(s), 3))
  }))
}
```

### Explicit Runge Kutta methods

The explicit methods are the right choice for nonstiff problems.
`Tsit5()` is the recommended default; `DP5()` is the classic
Dormand Prince pair; `BS3()` is cheap at loose tolerances; `Vern7()` and
`Vern9()` are efficient at tight tolerances. The low order methods
`Euler()`, `Midpoint()`, `Heun()`, `Ralston()` and `RK4()` are mostly of
didactic interest. `Euler()` always takes the fixed step `dt`; the others
carry an error estimate and adapt the step unless `adaptive = FALSE`, which
is used here to compare them at the same step.

```{r}
compare(osc, list(BS3(), Tsit5(), DP5(), Vern7(), Vern9()), err,
        reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-10)
compare(osc, list(Euler(), Midpoint(), Heun(), Ralston(), RK4()), err,
        dt = 0.01, adaptive = FALSE)
```

The two stage methods `Midpoint()`, `Heun()` and `Ralston()` give the same
error: on a linear problem every explicit two stage method of order two has
the same stability polynomial, so they produce identical steps.

Strong stability preserving methods (`SSPRK22()`, `SSPRK33()`,
`SSPRK432()` and others) keep the monotonicity properties of forward Euler
under a step size restriction, which matters for hyperbolic PDEs. The
low storage methods (`CarpenterKennedy2N54()`, `ORK256()`, the
`CKLLSRK*`, `DGLDDRK*` and `NDBLSRK*` families) need only two or three
registers per state.

```{r}
compare(osc, list(SSPRK22(), SSPRK33(), SSPRK432(), CarpenterKennedy2N54(), ORK256()), err,
        dt = 0.01, adaptive = FALSE)
```

### Stiff solvers

A problem is stiff when stability rather than accuracy limits the step of
an explicit method. On the heat equation `Tsit5()` is held to small steps
by stability long after the solution has become smooth, while the implicit
methods take steps limited only by accuracy:

```{r}
compare(heat, list(Tsit5(), Rodas5P(), KenCarp4(), FBDF()), heat_err,
        reltol = 1e-6, abstol = 1e-8)
```

The main families of implicit methods are:

* **Rosenbrock** methods (`Rosenbrock23()`, `Rodas4()`, `Rodas5P()` and many
  more) solve one linear system per stage instead of a nonlinear one.
  `Rodas5P()` is a strong default for small and medium stiff systems, and
  `Rosenbrock23()` at loose tolerances.
* **SDIRK** methods (`ImplicitEuler()`, `Trapezoid()`, `TRBDF2()`,
  `Kvaerno4()`, `KenCarp4()` and others) solve a nonlinear system per stage
  with Newton's method; the `KenCarp*` methods are also IMEX methods.
* **BDF** multistep methods (`FBDF()`, `QNDF()`, `ABDF2()` and
  `NordsieckBDF()`) reuse past steps and scale best to large systems.
* **Fully implicit Runge Kutta** methods, `RadauIIA3()`, `RadauIIA5()`,
  `RadauIIA9()` and `AdaptiveRadau()`, have very high order and excel at
  tight tolerances.
* **Extrapolation** methods (`ImplicitEulerExtrapolation()`,
  `ImplicitHairerWannerExtrapolation()`, and the explicit
  `ExtrapolationMidpointDeuflhard()`) vary their order adaptively.

```{r}
compare(heat, list(Rosenbrock23(), TRBDF2(), QNDF(), RadauIIA5(),
                   ImplicitEulerExtrapolation()), heat_err, reltol = 1e-6, abstol = 1e-8)
```

### Exponential integrators

Exponential integrators treat the linear part of the problem exactly with
matrix exponentials (computed by Krylov projection for the adaptive
`Exprb32()` and `Exprb43()`, and in the fixed step `Exp4()` and
`EXPRB53s3()`). These exponential Rosenbrock methods work with the full
Jacobian, so a plain `ODEProblem` is enough. On a linear problem they are
nearly exact.

```{r}
compare(heat, list(Exprb32(), Exprb43()), heat_err, reltol = 1e-6, abstol = 1e-8)
compare(heat, list(Exp4(), EXPRB53s3()), heat_err, dt = 0.01)
```

The fixed step exponential Runge Kutta methods (`LawsonEuler()`,
`NorsettEuler()`, `ETDRK4()`, `HochOst4()`) take a semilinear problem
$u' = A u + f(u, p, t)$, given as a `SplitODEProblem` whose first part is a
`MatrixOperator`. Here a constant source term is added to the heat
equation, and the errors are measured against a tight `Rodas5P()`
solution.

```{r}
src <- function(u, p, t) 0 * u + 1
forced <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) as.vector(lap %*% u) + 1, sin(pi * xs), c(0, 0.5))
ref <- solve(forced, Rodas5P(), reltol = 1e-10, abstol = 1e-12)
ref <- ref$u[[length(ref$t)]]
ref_err <- function(s) max(abs(s$u[[length(s$t)]] - ref))
semi <- SplitODEProblem(MatrixOperator(lap), src, sin(pi * xs), c(0, 0.5))
compare(semi, list(LawsonEuler(), NorsettEuler(), ETDRK4(), HochOst4()), ref_err, dt = 0.01)
```

The exponential time differencing methods (`NorsettEuler()`, `ETDRK4()`,
`HochOst4()`) integrate a constant source exactly, so their error is at
rounding level; the Lawson method, which exponentiates only the linear
part, is first order here.

### IMEX and multirate methods

A `SplitODEProblem(f1, f2, u0, tspan)` represents $u' = f_1(u) + f_2(u)$
where $f_1$ is stiff and $f_2$ is not. IMEX methods treat $f_1$
implicitly and $f_2$ explicitly: the additive `KenCarp*` methods, the
multistep `CNAB2()`, `CNLF2()` and `SBDF2()` to `SBDF4()`, and
`IMEXEuler()`. The multistep methods need a fixed `dt`.

```{r}
split <- SplitODEProblem(function(u, p, t) as.vector(lap %*% u), src,
                         sin(pi * xs), c(0, 0.5))
compare(split, list(KenCarp4(), CNAB2(), SBDF2(), IMEXEuler()), ref_err, dt = 0.01)
```

`KenCarp4()` is adaptive (`dt` is only its first step); the others take the
fixed step.

Multirate methods such as `MREEF()` take several small steps of the fast
part $f_1$ for each step of the slow part $f_2$; `nf` counts the
evaluations of $f_1$ and `nf2` those of $f_2$.

```{r}
fast_slow <- SplitODEProblem(function(u, p, t) c(-10 * u[1] + u[2], -u[2]),
                             function(u, p, t) c(0.1 * sin(t), 0.1 * u[1]),
                             c(1, 1), c(0, 1))
mr <- solve(fast_slow, MREEF(), dt = 0.1)
unlist(mr$stats[c("nf", "nf2")])
```

### Stabilized explicit methods

Runge Kutta Chebyshev methods, `RKC()`, `ROCK2()`, `ROCK4()`, `SERK2()` and
`ESERK4()`, are explicit methods with stability regions stretched along the
negative real axis. They suit large, moderately stiff problems with real
eigenvalues, like diffusion, where no linear algebra is wanted; the number
of stages adapts to a running estimate of the spectral radius.

```{r}
compare(heat, list(RKC(), ROCK4()), heat_err, reltol = 1e-6, abstol = 1e-8)
```

## Automatic stiffness detection and the default algorithm

`AutoSwitch(nonstiff, stiff)` monitors a stiffness estimate and switches
between two methods; `AutoTsit5(alg)` and `AutoVern7(alg)` (also
`AutoVern6`, `AutoVern8`, `AutoVern9`) pair the named explicit method with a
stiff one, as in OrdinaryDiffEq.jl.

When no algorithm is given, `solve()` uses `DefaultODEAlgorithm()`, the
OrdinaryDiffEqDefault choice: it starts with `Tsit5()` (`Vern7()` when
`reltol < 1e-6`), and on stiffness switches to `Rosenbrock23()` (`Rodas5P()`
when `reltol < 1e-6`) for up to 50 states and `FBDF()` above. With a non
identity mass matrix it uses `Rodas5P()` or `FBDF()` throughout.
`sol$alg_choice` records the method of each step (1 Tsit5, 2 Vern7,
3 Rosenbrock23, 4 Rodas5P, 5 FBDF). For an `AutoSwitch()` algorithm it is
1 for the nonstiff and 2 for the stiff method.

```{r}
table(solve(osc)$alg_choice)
table(solve(heat)$alg_choice)
table(solve(heat, AutoTsit5(Rodas5P()))$alg_choice)
```

The oscillator never leaves `Tsit5()`; on the heat equation the first
steps are taken with `Tsit5()` while the transient is resolved, and the
stiff method takes over once stability limits the step.

## DAE solvers

Differential algebraic equations arise naturally from acausal models. There
are two ways to solve them. When `mtkcompile()` leaves algebraic equations,
`ODEProblem()` builds a mass matrix problem, solved by the Rosenbrock
methods, `RadauIIA5()`, the BDF methods and the default algorithm.

```{r}
dae <- mtkcompile(System(list(D(x) ~ y, 0 ~ y^3 + y + x^3 + x), t, name = "dae"))
equations(dae)
mm_prob <- ODEProblem(dae, list(x ~ 1, y ~ -1), c(0, 2))
mm_prob$f$mass_matrix
mm_sol <- solve(mm_prob, Rodas5P())
c(tail(mm_sol[x], 1), exp(-2))
```

`DAEProblem()` builds the fully implicit form instead, solved by
`DFBDF()` (variable order BDF, the analogue of SUNDIALS IDA) and
`DImplicitEuler()`; initial derivatives are given as `D(x) ~ value`. The
default algorithm for a `DAEProblem` is `DFBDF()`.

```{r}
imp_prob <- DAEProblem(dae, list(x ~ 1, y ~ -1, D(x) ~ -1), c(0, 2))
sapply(list(DFBDF(), DImplicitEuler()), function(alg) {
  s <- solve(imp_prob, alg, reltol = 1e-6, abstol = 1e-8)
  c(steps = s$stats$naccept, x_end = tail(s[x], 1))
})
solve(imp_prob)$alg$name
```

## Solver options

### Automatic differentiation

Implicit methods need the Jacobian of the right hand side. By default it is
computed by forward mode automatic differentiation (`AutoForwardDiff()`),
which is exact. `AutoFiniteDiff()` uses finite differences (forward by
default, `AutoFiniteDiff("central")` for central ones), which costs extra
`f` evaluations. `AutoSparse(AutoForwardDiff())` detects the sparsity
pattern and colors the columns so that fewer directional derivatives are
needed; on this two state problem there is nothing to save, so its counts
match forward mode, and it pays off for large banded or sparse Jacobians.
System problems can also use the symbolic Jacobian with
`ODEProblem(sys, ..., jac = TRUE)`.

```{r}
vdp <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) c(u[2], 10 * (1 - u[1]^2) * u[2] - u[1]), c(2, 0), c(0, 6))
sapply(list(forward = AutoForwardDiff(), finite = AutoFiniteDiff(),
            sparse = AutoSparse(AutoForwardDiff())), function(ad) {
  s <- solve(vdp, Rodas5P(autodiff = ad), reltol = 1e-6, abstol = 1e-8)
  c(nf = s$stats$nf, njacs = s$stats$njacs, u1 = s$u[[length(s$t)]][1])
})
```

### Nonlinear solvers

The SDIRK methods solve their stage equations with the solver given by
`nlsolve`: `NLNewton()` (the default; `kappa` is the convergence
tolerance relative to the error tolerance and `max_iter` the iteration
limit), the fixed point iteration `NLFunctional()` and its Anderson
accelerated form `NLAnderson()`. The fixed point iterations need no
Jacobian, and so only converge on mildly stiff problems; Anderson
acceleration combines the previous iterates and here needs fewer function
evaluations than the plain iteration.

```{r}
mild <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) c(-20 * u[1] + u[2]^2, -u[2] + u[1]), c(1, 1), c(0, 1))
nl <- list(newton = NLNewton(), tight = NLNewton(kappa = 1e-6),
           functional = NLFunctional(), anderson = NLAnderson())
sapply(nl, function(n) {
  s <- solve(mild, TRBDF2(nlsolve = n))
  unlist(s$stats[c("nf", "njacs", "nsolve", "naccept")])
})
```

### Predictors

The initial guess of each stage solve is set by the `predictor` argument,
one of the values of `Predictor` (for instance `Predictor$Trivial`,
`Predictor$Linear`, the default of most SDIRK methods, or
`Predictor$MaxOrder`, which extrapolates the last step's interpolant). A
function `predictor(uprev, p, t, dt)` given to `NLNewton()` replaces the
guess at every stage.

```{r}
sapply(list(trivial = Predictor$Trivial, linear = Predictor$Linear,
            maxorder = Predictor$MaxOrder), function(pr) {
  s <- solve(mild, KenCarp4(predictor = pr))
  s$stats$nf
})
```

### Step limiters

A step limiter is a function `limiter(u, integ, p, t)` that returns the
state to keep after each accepted step, for instance a projection onto an
invariant. It is a `solve()` keyword, and also an
argument of the implicit and SSP constructors (`stage_limiter` for the
SSP and Rosenbrock methods acts after every stage). Here the oscillator is
projected onto the unit circle.

```{r}
proj <- function(u, integ, p, t) u / sqrt(sum(u^2))
free <- solve(osc, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-3, abstol = 1e-6)
kept <- solve(osc, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-3, abstol = 1e-6, step_limiter = proj)
c(free = max(abs(rowSums(free[]^2) - 1)), limited = max(abs(rowSums(kept[]^2) - 1)))
```

The `StepsizeLimiter(dtFE)` callback is different: it caps the step size
by a function `dtFE(u, p, t)`, such as a CFL condition, times a safety
factor of 9/10.

```{r}
capped <- solve(osc, Tsit5(), callback = StepsizeLimiter(function(u, p, t) 0.05))
max(diff(capped$t))
```

## Complex states

States may be complex, as for the Schrödinger equation. The explicit
methods work as they are. Implicit methods should be given
`AutoFiniteDiff()`: the forward mode duals are real, so with the default
`AutoForwardDiff()` the imaginary part of the Jacobian is discarded (with a
warning "imaginary parts discarded in coercion").

```{r}
H <- function(t) -1i * matrix(c(t, 1, 1, -t), 2)
lz <- ODEProblem(function(u, p, t) as.vector(H(t) %*% u), c(1 + 0i, 0), c(-1, 1))
zsol <- solve(lz, Tsit5(), reltol = 1e-8, abstol = 1e-10)
zsol(1)
sum(Mod(zsol(1))^2)
zimp <- solve(lz, Rosenbrock23(autodiff = AutoFiniteDiff()))
sum(Mod(zimp(1))^2)
```

## A stiff benchmark: the Robertson problem

The Robertson chemical kinetics problem is the classic stiff test: its rate
constants span nine orders of magnitude and the solution evolves over
$10^5$ time units. Comparing the statistics of several stiff solvers at the
same tolerances shows the trade offs: Rosenbrock methods compute a new
Jacobian on every step; BDF methods reuse it over many steps at the cost of
more, smaller steps; `RadauIIA5()` takes few large steps.

```{r}
rober <- function(u, p, t) {
  k1 <- p[1]; k2 <- p[2]; k3 <- p[3]
  c(-k1 * u[1] + k3 * u[2] * u[3],
    k1 * u[1] - k2 * u[2]^2 - k3 * u[2] * u[3],
    k2 * u[2]^2)
}
rprob <- ODEProblem(rober, c(1, 0, 0), c(0, 1e5), c(0.04, 3e7, 1e4))
rober_algs <- list(Rosenbrock23(), Rodas5P(), KenCarp4(), FBDF(), QNDF(), RadauIIA5())
rober_tab <- do.call(rbind, lapply(rober_algs, function(alg) {
  s <- solve(rprob, alg, reltol = 1e-6, abstol = 1e-8)
  u <- s$u[[length(s$t)]]
  data.frame(alg = alg$name, retcode = s$retcode, naccept = s$stats$naccept,
             nreject = s$stats$nreject, nf = s$stats$nf, njacs = s$stats$njacs,
             y3_end = signif(u[3], 6), mass = signif(sum(u), 10))
}))
rober_tab
```

All methods agree on the final state and conserve the total mass. The
default algorithm detects the stiffness after a few `Tsit5()` steps and
hands over to `Rosenbrock23()`:

```{r}
rdef <- solve(rprob)
table(rdef$alg_choice)
```

```{r}
rs <- solve(rprob, Rodas5P(), reltol = 1e-6, abstol = 1e-8)
ts <- 10^seq(-5, 5, length.out = 200)
Y <- rs(ts)
matplot(ts, Y * rep(c(1, 1e4, 1), each = length(ts)), type = "l", log = "x", lty = 1,
        xlab = "t", ylab = "concentration (y2 scaled by 1e4)")
legend("right", legend = c("y1", "1e4 y2", "y3"), col = 1:3, lty = 1, bty = "n")
```

## Julia equivalents

| Julia (SciML) | modelcompR |
|---|---|
| `ODEProblem(sys, op, tspan)` | `ODEProblem(sys, op, tspan)` |
| `prob[x]`, `prob.ps[a]` | `prob[x]`, `prob$ps[a]` |
| `prob.ps[a] = 2` | `prob$ps[a] <- 2` |
| `remake(prob; u0, p, tspan)` | `remake(prob, u0 = , p = , tspan = )` |
| `sol[x]`, `sol(t; idxs = x)` | `sol[x]`, `sol(t, idxs = x)` |
| `sol.t`, `sol.u`, `sol.stats`, `sol.retcode` | `sol$t`, `sol$u`, `sol$stats`, `sol$retcode` |
| `init`, `step!`, `solve!` | `init()`, `step_integrator()`, `solve_integrator()` |
| `reinit!`, `set_u!`, `add_tstop!`, `terminate!` | `reinit()`, `set_u()`, `add_tstop()`, `terminate()` |
| `EnsembleProblem`, `EnsembleSummary` | `EnsembleProblem()`, `EnsembleSummary()` |
| `Rodas5P(autodiff = AutoFiniteDiff())` | `Rodas5P(autodiff = AutoFiniteDiff())` |
| `KenCarp4(nlsolve = NLAnderson())` | `KenCarp4(nlsolve = NLAnderson())` |
